title: BiOCl Photocatalyst at Different Temperatures: TEM Insights into Structural Modifications and Photocatalytic Efficiency
content: In recent times, contamination of aquatic environments by emerging contaminants has become a critical environmental problem due to their persistence, toxicity, and potential risks to human health and ecosystems. These contaminants include pesticides, drugs, and antibiotics [1]. Pesticides are of particular concern, as they are widely used in agricultural activities and can accumulate in aquatic environments. One of the pesticides most used is 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid (2,4-D), a synthetic herbicide used to control weeds and pests. Due to its high solubility and resistance to conventional water treatment methods, the removal of 2,4-D from aqueous systems requires the development of advanced and efficient degradation techniques [2]. For the removal of these emerging pollutants in aquatic environments, several advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) have been developed as effective treatment strategies. AOPs are based on the generation of highly reactive species, hydroxyl radicals (•OH), which can degrade complex organic molecules into smaller and less toxic compounds [3]. Among them, heterogeneous photocatalysis has emerged as a particularly promising approach due to its ability to operate in diverse media, to be inexpensive, and easy to implement. Recently, bismuth oxyhalides (BiOX, X = Cl, Br, I) have gained significant attention as efficient photocatalysts due to their unique layered structure, efficient charge separation, and improved photocatalytic performance [4]. Among them, bismuth oxychloride (BiOCl) has shown promising activity under ultraviolet irradiation. The structural and morphological features of BiOCl play a crucial role in its photocatalytic efficiency, and temperature variations during synthesis or treatment can significantly affect its crystalline structure, surface area, and defect density. In this study, we investigated the structural evolution of the BiOCl photocatalyst at two different temperatures using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and analyzed the impact of these structural changes on its photocatalytic performance for 2,4-D degradation.
